title: Male Fertility Labs: WHO 2021 Semen Limits and Primary vs Secondary Hypogonadism
summary: Compare semen analysis results with the WHO 2021 lower reference limits, know when to test vitality, measure testosterone correctly, and use LH and FSH to separate testicular from pituitary failure.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 26 Hits 3, 4 and 13 and Trap 2. Checked against Boitrelle 2021 (WHO 6th edition review), Wang 2022 (WHO manual history) and Dandona & Rosenberg 2010. Hit 3 quotes “WHO 2010” values as volume 2–5 mL, concentration 15–50 million/mL, motility ≥ 40%, progressive ≥ 32%; the 2021 sixth edition lower limits are 1.4 mL, 42% and 30% (register flag rv-semen-who). Hit 13’s “< 300 ng/dL on two morning draws” is guideline-dependent (Dandona 2010 cites the Endocrine Society’s 300 ng/dL and AACE’s 200; current guidelines not read). Not taught: sperm concentration limit (16 × 10⁶/mL in the 6th edition is not in the sources read), the eosin-nigrosin colour detail, and the hCG stimulation test.

objectives: State the WHO 2021 lower reference limits for semen parameters and when to test vitality.
Explain why reference limits are not fertility thresholds.
Distinguish primary from secondary hypogonadism using LH and FSH.

scenes.title: A semen analysis and a low testosterone
scenes.altText: Two cards. Card A: a man in an infertile couple; semen volume 1.2 mL, total motility 35%, normal forms 3%. Card B: a 34-year-old with fatigue and low libido; morning total testosterone 210 ng/dL, LH and FSH high. A question token: “Which values are abnormal — and is B’s problem the testis or the pituitary?” The cartoon scientist holds a semen container and a hormone tube.

cues.text: Man A, in an infertile couple: semen volume 1.2 millilitres, total motility 35 percent, normal forms 3 percent.
Man B, 34, with fatigue and low libido: morning testosterone 210 nanograms per decilitre, and LH and FSH are high.
Which semen values fall below the reference limits? And is B’s problem in the testis or in the pituitary?

props.label: Below the limits? Testis or pituitary?

scenes.title: The axis and the reference limits
scenes.altText: A schematic hypothalamic–pituitary–testis axis: GnRH → pituitary LH and FSH → LH drives Leydig-cell testosterone; FSH supports spermatogenesis; testosterone feeds back to suppress LH. A reference card (WHO 2021, 6th edition: lower 5th centiles from men whose partners conceived within a year): volume 1.4 mL; total sperm number 39 × 10⁶ per ejaculate; total motility 42%; progressive motility 30%; vitality 54%; normal forms 4%. A note: these are lower reference limits, not thresholds for fertility.

cues.text: The testis answers to the pituitary. LH drives the Leydig cells to make testosterone; FSH supports sperm production. Testosterone feeds back to quieten LH.
Semen results are compared with WHO reference limits. The 2021 sixth edition uses the lower fifth centile of men whose partners conceived within a year.
Lower limits: volume 1.4 millilitres, total sperm number 39 million per ejaculate, total motility 42 percent, progressive motility 30 percent.
Vitality 54 percent, and normal forms by strict criteria 4 percent.
These are reference limits, not fertility thresholds. Men below them can father children, and men above them can be infertile.

scenes.title: Reading man A: what changed between editions
scenes.altText: A comparison card (WHO 2010 vs 2021 lower 5th centiles): volume 1.5 → 1.4 mL; total number 39 → 39 × 10⁶; total motility 40 → 42%; progressive 32 → 30%; vitality 58 → 54%; normal forms 4 → 4%. A vitality rule: the 6th edition recommends a vitality test when total motility is below 40% (the 5th edition tied it to progressive motility). Man A scored: volume 1.2 (below 1.4); total motility 35% (below 42%, and below 40% → vitality test); normal forms 3% (below 4%).

cues.text: The limits shifted slightly between the 2010 and 2021 editions. Volume went from 1.5 to 1.4 millilitres, total motility from 40 to 42 percent, and progressive motility from 32 to 30 percent.
Vitality moved from 58 to 54 percent. Total sperm number, 39 million, and normal forms, 4 percent, stayed the same.
The sixth edition also fixed a rule: test sperm vitality when total motility is below 40 percent.
Man A: volume 1.2 is below 1.4. Total motility 35 percent is below 42, and below 40, so a vitality test is indicated.
Normal forms 3 percent is below 4. Three values below the reference limits, which calls for a repeat analysis and clinical evaluation, not a verdict.

scenes.title: Low testosterone: testis or pituitary?
scenes.altText: A testosterone card: draw in the morning (circadian rhythm); no absolute cut-off — the Endocrine Society suggested 300 ng/dL (10.4 nmol/L) as the lower limit of normal, AACE 200 ng/dL; values 230–350 ng/dL may warrant a repeat with SHBG to calculate free testosterone (as summarized by Dandona 2010; newer guidelines not read). A split card: primary (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism — testicular failure: low testosterone + HIGH LH and FSH (e.g., Klinefelter syndrome, chemotherapy, radiation, injury); secondary (hypogonadotropic) — hypothalamic/pituitary: low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal LH/FSH. Back to the hook: B = primary testicular failure.

cues.text: Testosterone follows a daily rhythm, so draw it in the morning.

There is no single cut-off. A 2010 review cites the Endocrine Society’s 300 nanograms per decilitre as the lower limit of normal and AACE’s 200; borderline values of 230 to 350 may warrant a repeat with SHBG and calculated free testosterone.
Then look at LH and FSH. Low testosterone with high gonadotropins is primary, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: the testis has failed and the pituitary is shouting.
Causes include Klinefelter syndrome, chemotherapy, radiation and testicular injury.
Low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH is secondary: the hypothalamus or pituitary is not signalling. Man B, with high LH and FSH, has primary testicular failure.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Low testosterone + high LH/FSH → order a pituitary MRI” (✓ that is primary testicular failure); “One afternoon testosterone of 250 = hypogonadism” (✓ draw in the morning and repeat borderline values); “Total motility 41% is normal” (✓ below the WHO 2021 limit of 42% — but limits are not fertility cut-offs).

cues.text: Trap one: low testosterone with high LH and FSH, so order a pituitary scan. That pattern is primary testicular failure.
Trap two: a single afternoon testosterone of 250 proves hypogonadism. Draw in the morning, and repeat borderline values.
Trap three: total motility of 41 percent is normal. It is just below the 2021 limit of 42 percent, though reference limits are not fertility cut-offs.

scenes.title: High LH means the testis failed
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “If the pituitary is shouting (high LH/FSH), the testis isn’t listening — primary. If the pituitary is silent, look upstream — secondary.” A megaphone token and a muted token. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: if the pituitary is shouting, with high LH and FSH, the testis is not listening: primary. If the pituitary is silent, look upstream: secondary.
Where it breaks: mixed patterns occur, for example with obesity or ageing; SHBG changes alter total testosterone; and semen limits describe a population, not an individual’s fertility.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “WHO 2021 lower limits: volume 1.4 mL · total 39 × 10⁶ · total motility 42% · progressive 30% · vitality 54% · forms 4%”, “Morning testosterone; low T + high LH/FSH = primary; low/normal LH/FSH = secondary”.

cues.text: Compare semen results with the WHO 2021 lower limits, draw testosterone in the morning, and use LH and FSH to decide whether the testis or the pituitary has failed.

props.label: WHO 2021: 1.4 mL · 39 × 10⁶ · motility 42% · progressive 30% · vitality 54% · forms 4%
AM testosterone · T ↓ + LH/FSH ↑ = primary · LH/FSH low/normal = secondary

explanation.what: Plain language: semen analysis counts and checks sperm against reference limits from fertile men; hormone tests show whether low testosterone comes from the testis or from the brain’s signalling. Scientific terms: semen volume, total sperm number, total and progressive motility, vitality, normal forms (strict criteria), LH, FSH, primary (hypergonadotropic) and secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism, SHBG.
explanation.why: LH stimulates Leydig-cell testosterone; testosterone suppresses LH by negative feedback. Testicular failure removes feedback, so LH and FSH rise. Hypothalamic or pituitary failure leaves LH and FSH low or inappropriately normal.
explanation.measure: WHO 2021 lower 5th centiles: volume 1.4 mL, total number 39 × 10⁶/ejaculate, total motility 42%, progressive 30%, vitality 54%, normal forms 4%; vitality testing if total motility < 40%. Testosterone: morning sample; Endocrine Society (as cited 2010) 300 ng/dL (10.4 nmol/L); AACE 200 ng/dL; 230–350 ng/dL repeat with SHBG/free testosterone.
explanation.differs: Primary hypogonadism (high LH/FSH; e.g., Klinefelter, chemotherapy, radiation) vs secondary (low/normal LH/FSH; hypothalamic–pituitary). WHO 2010 vs 2021 limits.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: semen reference limits, vitality indication, LH/FSH pattern in primary vs secondary hypogonadism, and morning testosterone sampling.

comparisons.title: WHO 2010 vs 2021 lower limits
comparisons.distinguisher: Edition; both use 4% normal forms and 39 × 10⁶ total number.

mnemonic.explanation: High LH/FSH with low testosterone means primary testicular failure; a quiet pituitary points upstream.
mnemonic.limitation: Mixed patterns occur (obesity, ageing); SHBG changes alter total testosterone; semen limits describe a population, not an individual’s fertility.

analogyLimitations: Female reproductive testing and pregnancy markers are covered in other lessons.
takeaway: Compare semen results with the WHO 2021 lower limits, draw testosterone in the morning, and use LH and FSH to decide whether the testis or the pituitary has failed.

questions.stem: A semen analysis shows total motility 36%. According to the WHO 6th edition, which additional test is indicated?

options.rationale: Correct. The 6th edition recommends vitality assessment when total motility is below 40%.
Incorrect. Hormone testing may follow clinically, but the manual’s rule concerns vitality.

options.text: No further test; 36% is within limits
options.rationale: Incorrect. 36% is below the 42% lower limit.
Incorrect. Vitality testing distinguishes dead from immotile live sperm now.

questions.stem: A man has morning testosterone 180 ng/dL with markedly raised LH and FSH. Which is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. High gonadotropins with low testosterone indicate primary (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism.
Incorrect. Secondary hypogonadism shows low or inappropriately normal LH/FSH.
Incorrect. Markedly high LH/FSH with low testosterone is a primary pattern.
Incorrect. This is a classic physiological pattern.

questions.stem: Why should testosterone be measured in a morning sample?

options.rationale: Correct. Levels vary through the day; morning sampling standardizes interpretation.
Incorrect. The issue is physiological variation, not sample stability.

options.text: LH is only measurable in the morning
options.rationale: Incorrect. The timing recommendation is for testosterone.

options.text: Fasting is required for all hormone tests
options.rationale: Incorrect. The reason given is the circadian rhythm.

claims.text: WHO 2021 lower limits and 2010 comparison; vitality if total motility < 40%; limits from men whose partners conceived within a year.
Morning testosterone; 300 (ES, as cited) / 200 (AACE) ng/dL; borderline repeat with SHBG.
Primary: low T + high LH/FSH (Klinefelter, chemo, radiation); secondary: low/normal LH/FSH.
Sperm concentration 16 × 10⁶/mL; eosin-nigrosin stains dead sperm red; hCG stimulation raises T in secondary; two morning draws < 300 ng/dL (current guidelines).

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 3 labels volume 2–5 mL, concentration 15–50 million/mL, motility ≥ 40% and progressive ≥ 32% as “WHO 2010”; the WHO 2021 sixth edition lower limits are volume 1.4 mL, total motility 42% and progressive 30% (and WHO 2010’s volume limit was 1.5 mL). The lesson teaches WHO 2021.
